doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Church, the Black church's singing and the lack of live blues
summary: He heard the Black church's singing from outside and knew the blues only from records; no local blues players.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: She played piano at the church.
Was it a Baptist church?
I don’t know...

Methodist Church. Mose used to say when they wanted you to go to church, at least when you were married... The kids would say, “Daddy, aren’t you going?” You’d say... “Why aren’t you going?” You’d say, “Because it’s against my religion.” The church was the community, which was...
In the area, I guess there was a black church and a white church
Yeah. Well, the black church was...we didn’t have much to do with that.
And it’s still that way.
Yeah. It’s still that way.
In your church, did they do anything at all like the black church procedures, the singing... Or was it totally different?
I don’t know. I only heard the music, the singing from the black church, from the front of the black church. I remember hearing it, and...
Are you talking about the black church, honey?
Yes. I remember hearing the black church, the singing, you know...
That must have been a pretty powerful thing.

Yeah. Well, I don’t know how early I heard this, but it didn’t...I didn’t think of it as powerful or as any way... I didn’t think of it any way, you know... I don’t remember... This is all mixed up in my head.
But I also want to know this. Were there any people locally who would be playing the blues?
No.
Or itinerant musicians coming through.
No.
So for you, hearing the music of the black church was a live experience, and hearing the blues...you heard them on records.
Yeah, I heard the jukebox on records. There was a local player that was a blues player, and he moved out several years before I was... I met him one time, and... So I don’t remember much about him.
